items.title: James Moody — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: my -- my idol was Jimmy Dorsey. And then Charlie Barnett [phonetic sp.] then George Yald [phonetic sp.] then Ben [indiscernible], you know, like that, Buddy Tate [phonetic sp.].

ctx.x: Uh-huh. [affirmative] Yeah. So I went in 1943 and came out 1946, discharged. But, you know, it was different being -- just different being down South because there was a different mentality down there. Not only -- not only with so called Caucasians, but with the Negroes, too. It just did -- people thought differently, you know. There was a subservient attitude seen, you know. And I used to -- I used to be amazed, said, "Damn! items.title: James Moody interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998
items.q: well first of all, Jimmy Dorsey was my first inspiration, Jimmy Dorsey. So he played alto, so okay, well that could have been one of the reasons why I liked that. Then Charlie Barnet and Georgie Auld

ctx.x: Were people still playing, were they selling the C melodies back then too?

I don’t know, they probably were because I saw some, but the C melody, the C melody, no that wasn’t — and then again, I really didn’t know either alto or tenor. Like I just wanted a saxophone you see? And then when I went to the theater and saw Lester Young and — no I didn’t see Lester Young but I mean I heard him on the records with Count Basie — well first of all, Jimmy Dorsey was my first inspiration, Jimmy Dorsey. So he played alto, so okay, well that could have been one of the reasons why I liked that. Then…

said no I like that better than the others. Then I heard Coleman Hawkins, and Prez. Now when I heard Hawk, he didn’t knock me out like Lester Young did. But when I got older, I realized that Hawk was playing the changes better than Lester Young. But Lester Young had that beat and that sound, you know [scats]. Oh I like that boy.
